Olive-bellied sunbirds (Cinnyris chloropygius) begin life as altricial nestlings emerging from eggs that have been incubated over a developmental period. Data derived from the closely related Cinnyris jugularis indicate that hatching occurs after an incubation period of approximately 13 days [ab = approximately 13 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a thermal regime typical for many small passerines. Upon emergence, the hatchlings are extremely altricial and exhibit a very modest mass; field measurements of newly hatched chicks record an initial wet weight of just 0.84 grams [Ww0 = 0.84 grams]. This minimal body mass places the species at the lower end of the range documented for nectarivorous birds of comparable adult size and underscores the significant parental investment required to protect and provision such feeble young during the critical first days of life.

Sexual dimorphism in adult body size becomes apparent as the nestlings develop and ultimately reach their asymptotic mass. Following the rapid growth phase within the nest and the subsequent period of post-fledging development, adult females attain a maximum body mass of approximately 6.35 grams [Wwi = approximately 6.35 grams]. Adult males, by contrast, are noticeably heavier, reaching an ultimate wet weight of about 7.1 grams [Wwi = about 7.1 grams]. This disparity in mass is consistent with patterns observed across many sunbird species, where males often exhibit a slight size advantage, possibly linked to territorial defense and competition for floral resources. Both sexes undergo a pronounced physiological shift during this period of somatic maturation, transitioning from the metabolic demands of the growing juvenile stage to the maintenance requirements of the reproductively viable adult.

The developmental timeline from the nestling stage to independence and subsequent reproductive maturation follows a well-defined sequence, particularly when viewed under the thermal conditions that characterize the active metabolic state of these birds. At a body temperature typical of endothermic activity, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the fledging period is relatively brief; young birds achieve their first flight and depart the nest at 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching], a figure that is based on comparisons with the closely related Cinnyris jugularis. This rapid exodus from the nest is typical of sunbirds, as it reduces the risk of predation on the stationary brood. Following fledging, the juveniles undergo a continued period of parental provisioning and skill acquisition before reaching physiological independence and initiating their own reproductive cycles.

Reproductive maturation and the subsequent timing of first breeding are also tightly linked to the energetic conditions reflected by a body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal development and the capacity for gamete production, is reached relatively early in life; field data indicate that individuals become sexually mature at approximately 39 days after hatching [tp = approximately 39 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Despite this early physiological capability, the actual initiation of breeding is deferred. The time since birth at first brood is considerably longer, with birds typically producing their first clutch at around 365 days after hatching [tR = around 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This substantial delay between sexual maturity and first reproduction is a common life-history strategy among small passerines, likely reflecting the time required to establish a territory, secure a mate, and develop the foraging proficiency necessary to sustain the high energetic costs of egg production and chick rearing.
